title: Tone and Voice
bigQuestion: How can the same words mean one thing on the page and the opposite in the writer's mind, and how does a reader tell?

story.title: A Perfectly Reasonable Suggestion
story.kicker: In 1729 a respected Irish clergyman published a calm, well-organized essay proposing that poor families sell their babies as food.
paragraphs: Jonathan Swift was the dean of St. Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, a famous writer, and an angry man. Ireland in the 1720s was ruled from London, and its poor were desperately poor. Beggars crowded the roads with children they could not feed. Swift had written serious pamphlets about it, with serious proposals. Almost nobody in power had listened.

So in 1729 he published a short essay with a long title. It called itself a modest proposal for preventing the children of poor people from being a burden to their parents or country. The voice in the essay is calm and helpful. It sounds like an economist. It begins by describing the sad sight of beggars and their children, and says that anyone who could find a cheap and easy way to make those children useful would deserve a statue.

Then it makes its proposal. The writer has been assured, he says, by a knowledgeable American, that a healthy one-year-old child is a delicious and nourishing food, whether stewed, roasted, baked or boiled. He goes on to work out the numbers. He estimates how many children could be sold each year, at what price, and how much a family would earn. He notes that the skin could be made into gloves. He answers objections. He lists the advantages, one by one, in a perfectly organized paragraph.

Readers at the time were horrified, and then, a beat later, most of them understood. Swift did not want anyone to eat a child. He wanted his readers to notice that England's policies and Ireland's landlords were already treating the poor as things to be consumed. By saying the monstrous thing in the voice of a reasonable man, he made the reasonable men in his audience hear themselves. Near the end, he even slips in the real solutions he had proposed before, and has his narrator dismiss them as hopeless.

The essay works because of tone. Every word is calm; every idea is monstrous. The gap between the two is where the meaning lives. This chapter is about that gap: how writers control the feeling of their words, how a reader hears the difference between what a text says and what its writer means, and how you can build a voice of your own that sounds like nobody else.
story.think: Swift could have written a plain, angry essay saying that the poor were being treated like livestock. Why might the calm, monstrous version have hit harder?

lessons.title: Tone Is Not Mood
lessons.mainIdea: Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject; mood is the feeling the text creates in the reader, and the two can differ.
reading: Your phone buzzes: Fine. Do whatever you want. Those five words carry an attitude, and you can hear it even though no one spoke aloud. The attitude is not fine at all. That attitude, the writer's feeling toward the subject or the reader, is *tone*. Every text has one, from a textbook to a text message. In speech, tone lives in the voice. On the page, it has to be built out of words, and a reader who cannot hear it will misread almost everything.

Tone is different from *mood*. Mood is the feeling the text creates in the reader. The two often match: a warm tone makes a warm mood. But they can pull apart. Swift's tone in A Modest Proposal is calm, patient and practical. The mood in the reader is horror. That gap is on purpose. A horror story might be told in a cheerful tone to make the reader more uneasy, not less. When you describe a text, keep the two words separate. Tone belongs to the writer's attitude. Mood belongs to the reader's experience.

Naming tone takes precise words. Happy and sad are not enough. Is the tone bitter, playful, tender, mocking, weary, urgent, cold, admiring, sarcastic, matter-of-fact? Try to find a word that fits and one that almost fits, and explain the difference. A student who says the tone of the Gettysburg Address is serious is right but has said little. A student who says it is solemn, then resolute, has noticed that the tone moves. Tone is usually the first thing a reader feels and the last thing a reader can explain, and the skill of this chapter is closing that gap.

words.d: the writer's attitude toward the subject or the reader, as shown by the words
the feeling a text creates in the reader
a settled way of thinking or feeling about something

look.title: One Sentence, Four Tones
look.text: Four students write about the same event, a canceled field trip. One writes: The trip is canceled. Another: The trip, which we had planned since September, is canceled. Another: The trip is canceled, obviously. Another: The trip is canceled, and so, I suppose, is my faith in this institution.
look.prompt: Give each sentence a tone word, as precise as you can. Which one is sarcastic, and how do you know from the words alone?

check.q: What is the difference between tone and mood?
choices: Tone is for poems and mood is for stories
Tone is the reader's feeling and mood is the writer's
Tone and mood are two words for the same thing
Tone is the writer's attitude and mood is the feeling created in the reader
check.why: Tone belongs to the writer; mood belongs to the reader's experience. Swift's calm tone creates a horrified mood.

check.q: Why is serious a weak description of the tone of the Gettysburg Address?
choices: It is true but says little; solemn and resolute are more precise
The speech is actually humorous
Serious is not a real tone word
Tone cannot be described with a single word
check.why: Precise tone words, and noticing that the tone moves, tell the reader much more.

check.q: A horror story is told in a cheerful tone. According to the reading, what is the likely effect?
choices: The story becomes less frightening
The reader becomes more uneasy because of the gap
The story stops being horror
The reader cannot tell what happens
check.why: When tone and mood pull apart on purpose, the gap itself unsettles the reader.

lessons.title: Diction Builds Tone
lessons.mainIdea: Tone comes mostly from word choice: connotation, level of formality and how concrete or abstract the words are.
reading: Here are two sentences about the same dog. The animal was removed from the residence. And: They dragged the poor old dog out of his home. Same event. The first is cold, official, a little evasive; nobody in it seems responsible. The second is angry and sad. Nothing changed but the words. Removed became dragged; animal became poor old dog; residence became home. This is *diction* at work, and it is the main engine of tone.

Three features of diction do most of the work. First, *connotation*: the emotional charge a word carries. Slender and skinny describe the same body with opposite attitudes. Second, formality: whether the words are the kind you would use in a courtroom or a kitchen. Residence is formal; home is not. Formal diction tends to sound distant, careful, sometimes cold. Informal diction sounds close and personal, sometimes careless. Third, whether words are concrete or abstract. A thing you can see, dog, has more feeling in it than a category, animal.

Swift's diction is the secret of A Modest Proposal. He uses the words of trade and farming for human children: he speaks of breeders, of stock, of yield, of a child as a dish. Every one of those words is ordinary in a report about cattle. Put next to the word child, each becomes a small shock. The reader feels the tone go wrong before the argument does, and that feeling is the point. Swift is showing how the language of profit sounds when it is turned on people.

To analyze diction for tone, underline the five words in a passage that carry the most feeling. For each, write the plain, neutral version. Then describe what the writer's choice adds. If you cannot find a neutral version, that word may be doing more than you thought. This method also works in reverse for your own writing. If a paragraph you wrote sounds flat, find the neutral words and ask which ones deserve a charge.

words.d: a writer's choice of words
the feeling or association a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning
how official or careful, rather than casual, a piece of language is
naming an idea or category rather than a thing you can see or touch

look.title: Swift's Farmyard Words
look.text: Swift's narrator calculates the number of children born each year to poor parents, refers to the mothers as breeders, and reasons that a well-nursed child of one year is a most delicious and nourishing food. He suggests that one male be kept for every four females for breeding, exactly as farmers do with sheep and cattle.
look.prompt: List the words here that belong to farming. What does each one do to the reader when it is applied to a human being?

check.q: In the two dog sentences, what made the second one sound angry and sad?
choices: It was longer
It used a question mark
Words with strong connotations replaced cold, formal ones
It named the dog's owner
check.why: Dragged, poor old dog and home carry feeling that removed, animal and residence do not.

check.q: Which pair shows two words with the same meaning but opposite connotations?
choices: Dog and cat
Run and walk
Morning and evening
Slender and skinny
check.why: Both describe a thin body, but slender approves and skinny does not.

check.q: Why does Swift use farming words like breeders and stock for people?
choices: So the reader feels the language of profit turned on human beings
Because he did not know other words
To make the essay easier to read
Because his readers were mostly farmers
check.why: Each ordinary farmyard word becomes a shock next to the word child, and the wrongness of the tone is the message.

lessons.title: Syntax and Voice
lessons.mainIdea: Sentence length and shape, called syntax, give a writer's voice its rhythm and can change tone as much as words do.
reading: Read these two versions aloud. He looked at the letter. He read it. He put it down. And: Looking at the letter, he read it slowly, turning each line over in his mind, and then, with the care of a man who has decided something, he put it down. Same events. The first is clipped, tense, maybe cold. The second is slow, thoughtful, almost tender. The difference is *syntax*: the length of sentences, how they are built, and how they are arranged.

Short sentences feel urgent, blunt or certain. They land like steps. Long sentences feel reflective, flowing, sometimes grand, sometimes nervous, depending on how they are built. A long sentence that keeps piling on and, and, and feels breathless. A long sentence with careful clauses, each in its place, feels composed. Most strong writers mix the two, and the mix is a signature. Hemingway is famous for short ones. Dickens for long ones. Lincoln for a few long ones that end in something short.

Together, diction and syntax make a writer's *voice*: the sound of a particular mind on the page, the thing that lets you recognize a writer from one paragraph. Mark Twain's voice is plain words in long, easy, talking sentences that suddenly stop for a joke. Edgar Allan Poe's voice is nervous: dashes, exclamations, a narrator interrupting himself. Voice is not the same as tone. Tone changes with the subject. Voice stays, the way your friend's laugh stays even when the joke changes.

To hear syntax, count. Count the words in each sentence of a paragraph and write the numbers in a row. A run of eights and nines is one voice; a row like 31, 4, 27, 3 is another. Notice where the short sentence comes. Writers usually put it at the moment they want you to feel a stop. Then ask what the pattern does. A paragraph of long sentences that ends in three words is making a point with its shape, whether or not the reader notices why it felt strong.

words.d: the arrangement of words and the length and shape of sentences
the recognizable sound of a particular writer's mind on the page
a group of words with a subject and a verb

look.title: Words per Sentence in Two Model Paragraphs
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the two versions of the letter scene in this reading
look.prompt: Paragraph A has three short sentences; B has one long one. Which would you use to describe a car crash, and which to describe a slow walk home, and why?

check.q: What is syntax?
choices: The dictionary meaning of a word
The length, shape and arrangement of sentences
The feeling a text creates in a reader
A writer's use of humor
check.why: Syntax is about how sentences are built and ordered, not about which words are chosen.

check.q: According to the reading, how do short sentences tend to feel?
choices: Reflective and flowing
Grand and formal
Urgent, blunt or certain
Nervous and breathless
check.why: Short sentences land like steps. Long ones flow or pile up depending on their build.

check.q: How does the reading distinguish voice from tone?
choices: Voice is louder than tone
Voice is only in speech, tone only in writing
Voice is the reader's feeling and tone is the writer's
Tone changes with the subject, but voice stays recognizable
check.why: Voice is like a friend's laugh: it persists even when the joke, and the tone, change.

lessons.title: Irony: Saying the Opposite
lessons.mainIdea: Verbal irony means the opposite of what the words say, and readers detect it through context and tone clues.
reading: It is pouring rain, your bus is late and your shoes are soaked. Someone says, Great day. You do not correct them. You know they mean the reverse, and you know it instantly, from the situation and their face. That is *verbal irony*: saying one thing to mean its opposite. Sarcasm is verbal irony with an edge, aimed at someone. On the page there is no face, so a writer has to leave other clues, and a reader has to look for them.

The clues are usually a gap. The words say one thing; the facts around them say another. Swift's narrator calls his proposal modest and then proposes cannibalism. The word modest is ironic because the plan is the least modest thing imaginable. Praise that is far too big for its object is a clue: a writer who calls a broken pencil a magnificent instrument does not mean it. So is calm about something that should cause alarm. So is a narrator who reveals more than he realizes, as when Swift's narrator mentions that he cannot profit from his own plan because his children are too old.

There are two other kinds of irony worth knowing. *Situational irony* is when what happens is the opposite of what was expected, such as a fire station burning down. *Dramatic irony* is when the audience knows something a character does not, so that the character's words mean more than the character intends. Neither is about tone exactly, but both create it. A story full of dramatic irony feels tense or sad, because the reader is watching someone walk toward a door they cannot see.

Irony is the device most often missed by readers, and missing it flips the meaning of a text. A reader who takes Swift literally thinks he is a monster. A reader who misses the irony in a friend's text starts a fight. When something in a text seems too strange, too calm or too extreme to be meant, stop and ask whether the writer is saying the opposite. That pause is the whole skill. Irony does not announce itself; it waits for a reader who is paying attention.

words.d: saying one thing while meaning the opposite
when what happens is the opposite of what was expected
when the audience knows something a character does not
verbal irony with a mocking or cutting edge

look.title: The Review
look.text: A restaurant review, written for this lesson: The service was remarkable. Our waiter visited us twice in ninety minutes, and both times he remembered that we existed. The soup arrived at a temperature that could not possibly burn anyone. I have rarely left a restaurant so hungry, or so grateful for the experience.
look.prompt: Find every clue that the reviewer means the opposite of what the words say. Which single word does the most ironic work?

check.q: Why is the word modest ironic in Swift's title?
choices: Swift was a humble man
The proposal is the least modest thing imaginable
Modest meant something different in 1729
The essay is very short
check.why: The plan is to eat children, the least modest idea imaginable. The gap between the word and the plan is verbal irony.

check.q: A fire station burns down. Which kind of irony is this?
choices: Verbal irony
Sarcasm
Dramatic irony
Situational irony
check.why: The outcome is the opposite of what anyone would expect from a fire station.

check.q: What does the reading say a reader should do when a text seems too calm or too extreme to be meant?
choices: Assume the writer made a mistake
Skip the passage
Stop and ask whether the writer means the opposite
Look up the writer's biography
check.why: Irony waits for an attentive reader. The pause to ask is the whole skill.

lessons.title: Satire: Laughing to Wound
lessons.mainIdea: Satire uses irony, exaggeration and mockery to expose a real fault, and it always has a target and a purpose.
reading: A joke is meant to make you laugh. *Satire* is meant to make you laugh and then feel a sting, because the joke is aimed at something real: a leader, a habit, an institution, a way of thinking. Swift's essay is satire. Its target is not the poor, and not really the narrator. Its target is a society that talked about poverty in the cold language of profit and did nothing. The laughter, if you can call it that, is meant to shame.

Satire has tools. Irony is the main one: the writer pretends to hold a view in order to expose it. *Exaggeration* is another: taking a real tendency and pushing it past the point of sanity, so that its shape becomes visible. Society was already treating the poor as economic units; Swift pushed that one step further, to eating them. A third tool is the *persona*, an invented speaker who is not the author. Swift's narrator, the calm projector with his tables of figures, is a mask. Reading satire well means seeing the author's face behind it.

Mark Twain was the great American satirist of the 1800s. In a short piece called Advice to Youth, given as a talk in 1882, he pretends to give young people the usual moral guidance and undermines each piece as he gives it. He tells them to obey their parents when their parents are present. He tells them that a lie told carelessly is a disgrace, so they should practice. The persona is a solemn old moralist; the target is the empty way adults lecture the young. The reader laughs, then notices that Twain has a point.

Because satire says the opposite of what it means, it is often misread, and satirists have been punished for jokes their readers took straight. That is worth remembering online, where a satirical post gets shared without its context and becomes, for many readers, a sincere one. When you meet a text that seems outrageous, look for the target. If there is one, and the exaggeration exposes something true about it, you are probably reading satire. If the outrage is the whole point, you are probably not.

words.d: writing that uses irony, exaggeration and mockery to expose a real fault
making something seem larger or more extreme than it is, for effect
an invented speaker or mask a writer adopts, distinct from the author
the person, habit or institution a satire is aimed at

look.title: Twain Advises the Young
look.text: In his 1882 talk, Twain advises young people to obey their parents when the parents are present, since that is the safest policy and the parents will make them obey anyway. He tells them to get up with the lark, and suggests they train a lark to get up at half past nine. He warns that a careless lie is a disgrace, so they must practice lying diligently until they are good at it.
look.prompt: Each piece of advice starts sincerely and then turns. What is Twain's real target, and what does the persona of the wise old adviser let him do?

check.q: What is the target of Swift's satire?
choices: The poor families of Ireland
The narrator's cooking
A society that treated the poor as economic units and did nothing
American visitors to London
check.why: The essay pushes the real habit of talking about people as profit one step further, to expose it.

check.q: What is a persona in satire?
choices: The reader the writer imagines
The title of the essay
The moral of the story
An invented speaker who is a mask for the author
check.why: Swift's calm projector and Twain's solemn moralist are masks; the author's face is behind them.

check.q: Why is satire often misread online, according to the reading?
choices: A satirical post is shared without its context and taken as sincere
Satire cannot be written in short form
Most people online do not read Twain
Satire is illegal in some countries
check.why: Because satire says the opposite of what it means, it needs context, and sharing strips context away.

lessons.title: Understatement and Overstatement
lessons.mainIdea: Saying less than the truth or far more than it are both tone tools, and both depend on the reader knowing the real size of the thing.
reading: A student walks in an hour late, soaked, having missed the bus, fallen in a puddle and lost her homework, and says, Rough morning. That is *understatement*: saying much less than the situation deserves. The gap between the small words and the large fact is where the effect lives. Understatement can be funny, brave or bitter, depending on the situation, but it always sends the same signal: the speaker is in control of feelings that could have overflowed.

Overstatement, also called *hyperbole*, runs the other way. I have told you a million times. That backpack weighs a ton. Nobody takes the number literally, and nobody is meant to. Hyperbole is the natural language of anger, joy and exhaustion, and it is everywhere in advertising, which is a reason to notice it there. In careful writing it works best when it is clearly a joke or clearly a feeling. When a writer means it as evidence, it is a fallacy, and the next chapter will have more to say about that.

Twain used both. In 1897 a newspaper reported that he was dying or already dead, when in fact it was his cousin who was ill. He wrote back that the report of his death was an exaggeration. The line is remembered because of its understatement: a false report of your own death is a great deal more than an exaggeration, and the calm word makes the reader laugh. Twain's travel writing, on the other hand, is full of cheerful hyperbole about mountains, coachmen and hotel bills.

Both devices require the reader to know the real size of the thing. Rough morning is only understatement if you know about the puddle. That means writers must give the facts before or after the small or huge words, and readers must check the facts against the words. When you find a claim that seems far too small or far too big, ask which it is, and then ask what tone it creates. The answer is often the key to the whole passage.

words.d: deliberately saying less than the situation deserves
deliberate exaggeration for effect, not meant literally
meaning exactly what the words say, with no figure of speech

look.title: The Report of His Death
look.text: In 1897, when a newspaper printed that Twain was dying in London, a reporter came to ask about it. Twain explained that the confusion came from his cousin's illness, and said that the report of his death was an exaggeration. The line is usually misquoted today as reports of my death are greatly exaggerated.
look.cite: Mark Twain, responding to a newspaper report, London, 1897 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why is the calm word exaggeration funnier than an angry denial would have been? What does the understatement tell you about Twain's attitude?

check.q: Which sentence is an example of understatement?
choices: I have never been so angry in my entire life.
After the tornado tore off the roof, Dad said the house needed a little work.
This is the best pizza in the universe.
The test was hard.
check.why: A torn-off roof is far more than a little work. The gap between small words and a large fact is understatement.

check.q: When does the reading say hyperbole becomes a problem?
choices: When it is used in a joke
When it appears in a poem
When a writer means it as evidence
When it involves numbers
check.why: Exaggeration as a feeling is fine; exaggeration offered as proof is a fallacy.

check.q: What must a reader know for understatement to work?
choices: The real size of the thing being described
The writer's date of birth
The dictionary definition of every word
Whether the writer is famous
check.why: Rough morning is only understatement if you know about the puddle and the lost homework.

lessons.title: Formal and Informal Registers
lessons.mainIdea: A register is the level of language a situation calls for, and choosing the wrong one is a tone mistake even when every word is correct.
reading: You do not talk to your grandmother the way you talk to your teammates, and you do not text a friend the way you write a college application. Each situation has a *register*: a level of language, from very formal to very casual, that fits it. Formal register uses complete sentences, standard grammar, precise vocabulary and no slang. Informal register allows contractions, sentence fragments, slang and inside jokes. Neither is better. A wedding toast in legal language and a court filing in text-speak are both failures.

Register is a tone decision that most people make without noticing. That is fine until the situation is new. A student emailing a teacher for the first time often reaches for the register of a group chat, hey can u send the hw, and the teacher hears disrespect that the student did not intend. The words were not wrong. The register was. The fix is not to sound fancy; it is to match the room: Hello Ms. Ortiz, could you send the homework from Tuesday? Thank you.

Writers also switch registers on purpose, for effect. A formal essay that drops one plain, blunt sentence, such as This is wrong, gains force from the drop. A casual voice that suddenly goes formal can sound ironic, as when a friend says I regret to inform you that we are out of chips. Twain is a master of this. His narrators speak plainly and then produce a grand phrase, and the mismatch is the joke. Swift does the reverse: a formal register the whole way, applied to something no formal register should touch.

When you write, decide the register before the first sentence, based on audience and purpose. Then hold it, except where you break it on purpose. When you read, notice the register and ask whether it fits. A politician who speaks to a crowd of farmers in the register of a law lecture has made a rhetorical error, and a reader who notices can say exactly what went wrong.

words.d: the level of formality in language that a situation calls for
very informal words used by a particular group, often short-lived
a shortened form such as can't or I'm

look.title: Two Emails
look.text: Email one: hey i wasnt there friday can u tell me what i missed. Email two: Dear Mr. Banks, I was absent on Friday because of a doctor's appointment. Could you let me know what I missed and whether there is anything I should complete before Monday? Thank you for your time.
look.prompt: Both emails ask the same thing. What exactly does the second one do differently, and what would the teacher assume about each writer?

check.q: What is a register?
choices: A list of words a writer uses most
The level of formality a situation calls for
The mood of a story
A device for recording speech
check.why: Register runs from very formal to very casual, and the right one depends on audience and purpose.

check.q: A student writes hey can u send the hw to a teacher. What went wrong, according to the reading?
choices: The grammar was wrong
The student was rude on purpose
The register did not match the situation
The message was too long
check.why: The words were not wrong in themselves, but the casual register sent a message the student did not intend.

check.q: Why might a formal essay drop in one blunt, plain sentence?
choices: The drop in register gives the sentence force
The writer ran out of formal words
Blunt sentences are required by essay rules
It makes the essay shorter
check.why: A switch in register on purpose draws attention to the sentence where it happens.

lessons.title: Tone in Letters and Editorials
lessons.mainIdea: Persuasive nonfiction, from an editorial to a letter, chooses a tone to fit its reader, and the tone is part of the argument.
reading: An *editorial* is an opinion piece in a newspaper, written to persuade readers about a public question. A letter to the editor is a reader's reply. Both are arguments, but their tone is a choice as important as their evidence. A calm, measured editorial invites the reader to reason alongside it. A furious one invites the reader to feel with it or reject it. Neither is automatically right. The tone must fit the subject, the reader and the paper.

Read the opening of an editorial and ask what it assumes about you. A sentence like Anyone who has waited for a Chicago bus in January knows the problem assumes you are a neighbor and a fellow sufferer; the tone is companionable. A sentence like The council's decision is indefensible assumes you are a judge who will weigh the case; the tone is prosecutorial. A sentence like It is time we stopped pretending assumes you share the writer's frustration; the tone is impatient. Each opening picks a relationship with the reader and holds it.

Letters, public and private, work the same way. Lincoln wrote in 1862 to Horace Greeley, a newspaper editor who had attacked him in print. Lincoln's reply was published. Its tone is patient and almost gentle, even though the subject was the most explosive question of the war. He says that if he could save the Union without freeing any slave he would, and if he could save it by freeing all of them he would, and if he could save it by freeing some and leaving others alone he would do that. The measured tone was aimed past Greeley at a divided public, and it was itself an argument: that the president was thinking, not raging.

When you analyze a persuasive letter or editorial, name the tone in a precise word or two, find three phrases that create it, and then ask the important question: how does this tone help the argument reach this reader? A furious tone can be exactly right for readers who are already angry and need to be organized. A gentle tone can be exactly right for readers who expect an attack. The tone is never decoration. It is a decision about who the reader is.

words.d: an opinion piece in a newspaper that argues for a position on a public question
calm, careful and controlled in tone
sounding like a lawyer building a case against someone

look.title: Lincoln Answers an Editor
look.text: My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union, and is not either to save or to destroy slavery. If I could save the Union without freeing any slave I would do it, and if I could save it by freeing all the slaves I would do it; and if I could save it by freeing some and leaving others alone I would also do that.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862
look.prompt: Describe the tone in two precise words. Which features of the syntax, the repeated if clauses, help create it, and who beyond Greeley was meant to hear it?

check.q: What does an editorial's opening sentence do, according to the reading?
choices: It states the newspaper's name
It lists the evidence to come
It always asks a question
It picks a relationship with the reader and holds it
check.why: Each opening assumes something about the reader, neighbor, judge or fellow sufferer, and sets the tone accordingly.

check.q: Why was Lincoln's measured tone to Greeley itself an argument?
choices: It showed a divided public that the president was thinking, not raging
It proved that Greeley was wrong about the facts
It made the letter shorter
It used more formal words than Greeley did
check.why: The calm tone was aimed past Greeley at the public, and the calm was the message.

check.q: When could a furious tone be the right choice for an editorial?
choices: Never; editorials must always be calm
When the readers are already angry and need to be organized
When the writer has no evidence
When the newspaper is small
check.why: Tone is a decision about who the reader is, and angry readers may need a voice that matches them.

lessons.title: When the Tone Shifts
lessons.mainIdea: Many texts change tone partway through, and the moment of the shift is usually where the meaning turns.
reading: Douglass spends the first part of his Fourth of July speech in a tone of respect, even admiration, for the founders. Then, in a sentence, he changes. Pardon me, he asks, why am I called to speak here today? The tone becomes sharp, then furious, then, near the end, hopeful. A reader who marks only one tone for the speech has missed its engine. The *shift* is where the argument happens.

Tone shifts are usually marked. Look for a but, a yet, a question, a one-line paragraph, a change of pronoun, a sudden short sentence after long ones. Look for a change in diction, from grand words to plain ones or the reverse. Lincoln's Second Inaugural moves from a flat, almost bored tone about how little needs to be said, to a solemn tone about God's judgment, to the tender last sentence. Each turn is signaled by a change in sentence length and word choice, and each turn does something to the audience.

Swift's essay has a shift so quiet that many readers miss it. Near the end, the narrator lists other remedies, the ones Swift had seriously proposed in earlier writing: taxing absentee landlords, buying Irish goods, learning to love the country. The narrator says he does not want to hear of these, since there is no hope anyone will try them. For one paragraph the mask slips. The tone under the calm is exhausted and bitter, and a reader who catches it has found Swift's actual face.

When you analyze a text, draw a line where the tone changes and label the tone on each side. Then ask two questions. What signals the shift? And what does the shift do to the reader? Often the answer to the second question is the thesis of your whole essay. A text that moves from praise to attack is making its audience feel the fall. A text that moves from attack to hope is offering a way out. The shape of the tone is the shape of the argument.

words.d: a change in tone, subject or approach partway through a text
a word or feature that marks where a change happens
serious and dignified in tone

look.title: Find the Turn
look.text: A paragraph written for this lesson: Our school has a proud history. The trophy case is full. The alumni wall is long. The band has marched in three parades this year alone. And yet a freshman with a reading disability waited nine weeks this fall for the help her plan promised her, because no one was there to give it.
look.prompt: Where exactly does the tone shift, what word signals it, and how does the shift make the reader feel about the trophy case?

check.q: What does the reading say about a reader who marks only one tone for Douglass's speech?
choices: They have found its main idea
They have read it correctly
They have missed its engine, since the shift is where the argument happens
They have confused tone with mood
check.why: The speech moves from respect to fury to hope, and the movement is the argument.

check.q: Which of these is named as a signal of a tone shift?
choices: A sudden short sentence after long ones
A page number
The title of the text
A footnote
check.why: Shifts are marked by words like but and yet, questions, pronoun changes and changes in sentence length or diction.

check.q: Where does the reading say Swift's mask slips?
choices: In the title
In the paragraph where the narrator dismisses the real remedies
In the first sentence about beggars
In the description of the American
check.why: When the narrator says there is no hope anyone will try the real solutions, Swift's bitterness shows through.

lessons.title: Reading Twain for Voice
lessons.mainIdea: Twain's voice comes from plain diction, talking syntax and a deadpan turn, and studying it shows how a voice is made of choices.
reading: Samuel Clemens grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River. He worked as a riverboat pilot, and he took the name Mark Twain from the leadsman's call for two fathoms of water. He wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer in 1876 and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn in 1884. In the second book he did something new in American literature. He let a poor, uneducated boy tell the whole story in his own words. The voice was the point. Readers had never heard a book sound like that.

Three things make Twain's voice. First, plain diction: short common words, the ones people actually say, with the occasional grand word dropped in for comic effect. Second, a talking syntax: long sentences strung together with and, the way a person tells a story out loud, with a short sentence when the story needs to stop. Third, the deadpan turn: a sentence that sets up something serious and ends somewhere absurd, delivered with a straight face. The reader does the laughing; the narrator never does.

Twain also wrote about voice directly. In a letter of 1888 he said that the difference between the almost right word and the right word is a large matter, as large as the difference between the lightning bug and the lightning. That is the plainest statement of a stylist's creed ever written, and it is itself an example. He could have said precise diction matters. Instead he gave you a bug and a bolt of lightning.

To learn from a voice, imitate it. Take a paragraph of your own and rewrite it the way Twain would tell it: plain words, one long talking sentence, one deadpan turn at the end. Then rewrite it as Poe would, nervous and full of dashes. You will not write like either of them for long. But you will discover that your own voice is also made of choices, and that you can make them on purpose.

words.d: delivered with no show of emotion, so the humor comes from the straight face
a writer especially skilled in the art of choosing and arranging words
to copy a model closely in order to learn from it

look.title: A Nervous Voice
look.text: True! — nervous — very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?
look.cite: Edgar Allan Poe, opening of The Tell-Tale Heart, 1843
look.prompt: Count the dashes and the repeated words in this one sentence. What do they tell you about the speaker before he has told you a single fact?

check.q: What was new about Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, according to the reading?
choices: It was the first American novel
It was written entirely in verse
It was set on the Mississippi River
A poor, uneducated boy tells the whole story in his own voice
check.why: Letting Huck narrate in his own words was the point; readers had never heard a book sound like that.

check.q: What is a deadpan turn in Twain's writing?
choices: A serious setup that ends somewhere absurd, delivered with a straight face
A very long sentence with no punctuation
A description of a river
A paragraph written entirely in dialect
check.why: The narrator never laughs; the reader does. That straight face is the deadpan.

check.q: Why does the reading call Twain's lightning-bug line an example of its own point?
choices: Because it is about weather
Because it is very short
Because instead of an abstract statement it gives a concrete image
Because it was written in a letter
check.why: He could have said precise diction matters. Instead he chose the exact, vivid words: a bug and a bolt.

lessons.title: Developing a Voice of Your Own
lessons.mainIdea: Your writing voice is built from choices you already make in speech, and you strengthen it by writing plainly, reading aloud and cutting what is not yours.
reading: Many students believe they have no writing voice. They do. It shows up in the story they tell at lunch, in the text they send when something goes wrong, in the way they argue with a sibling. Those are all voices, made of diction and syntax and attitude. The problem is not that the voice is missing. The problem is that school writing often trains students to hide it behind words they would never say: utilize, in conclusion, the aforementioned. A voice cannot be heard through a costume.

The first step, then, is subtraction. Write a draft. Read it aloud. Every time you hit a phrase you would never say out loud to a friend, mark it. Some of those phrases belong; formal writing has its register. But most of them are borrowed, and borrowed words sound borrowed. Replace them with the word you would actually use, and see if the sentence gets stronger. It usually does. Twain's lightning-bug rule applies here: the almost-right word is often the one you reached for because it sounded like writing.

The second step is addition, and it is harder. A voice needs a point of view: something you notice that others do not, an attitude toward the subject, a willingness to say a plain thing plainly. It also needs rhythm. Vary your sentence lengths. Put the short sentence where the stop belongs. Let one long sentence run when the thought runs. Read writers whose voices you like, and notice what they do, and steal the moves without stealing the words.

The third step is honesty about register. A strong voice is not the same as an informal one. Lincoln's voice at Gettysburg is formal, and it is unmistakably his. What makes a voice is not slang but control: the writer chose every word, and you can feel it. So choose. Decide your tone before you begin. Hold it. Break it once if the break is earned. And read your writing aloud, always, because the ear catches what the eye forgives.

words.d: the position or attitude from which a writer sees and describes a subject
removing words that do not belong, as a step in revision
the sense that a writer chose every word on purpose

look.title: The Costume Draft
look.text: A student's first sentence: In today's modern society, it is imperative that individuals utilize their time in an efficient manner. Her spoken version, when a friend asked what she meant: People waste hours every day and then say they had no time. Same idea. One of them sounds like a person.
look.prompt: Which sentence has a voice, and what specific words in the other one are the costume? Rewrite the first sentence a third way, keeping a formal register but sounding like a human being.

check.q: What does the reading say is the real problem for students who think they have no voice?
choices: They do not talk enough
School writing has trained them to hide their voice behind borrowed words
They have not read enough Twain
Their sentences are too short
check.why: The voice exists in their speech; it is covered by a costume of words they would never say.

check.q: What is the first step the reading recommends?
choices: Adding more descriptive adjectives
Writing in slang
Memorizing famous speeches
Reading a draft aloud and replacing phrases you would never say
check.why: Subtraction comes first: find the borrowed words and replace them with the ones you would actually use.

check.q: According to the reading, what makes a voice strong?
choices: Control: the sense that the writer chose every word
Informal language throughout
Very long sentences
Avoiding any formal register
check.why: Lincoln's voice is formal and still unmistakably his. Strength comes from choice, not slang.

review.q: Swift's tone in A Modest Proposal is calm, and the reader feels horror. Which statement is correct?
choices: The tone is horror and the mood is calm
Tone and mood are the same here
The mood is calm because the narrator is calm
The tone is calm and the mood is horror, and the gap is deliberate
review.why: Tone belongs to the writer's attitude; mood is the reader's feeling. Swift pulls them apart on purpose.

review.q: Which change in a sentence most directly changes its tone through diction?
choices: Replacing removed with dragged
Adding a comma
Making the sentence a question
Putting it in a new paragraph
review.why: Swapping a neutral word for one with a strong connotation is diction at work.

review.q: A paragraph of long sentences ends with a three-word sentence. What is this an example of?
choices: Situational irony
Syntax used for effect
Hyperbole
A register error
review.why: Sentence length and arrangement, syntax, create emphasis where the short sentence lands.

review.q: Which of these is dramatic irony?
choices: Calling a rainy day great
A police station is robbed
The audience knows the letter is fake, but the character trusts it
A student says a flood was a bit damp
review.why: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something a character does not.

review.q: What must satire always have, according to the chapter?
choices: A happy ending
A first-person narrator
Rhyme
A real target and a purpose
review.why: Satire aims its laughter at a real fault; without a target it is just a joke.

review.q: A student emails a teacher: yo whats on the test. What kind of mistake is this?
choices: A register mistake
A spelling mistake only
A mood mistake
A dramatic irony mistake
review.why: The level of formality did not match the situation, which is a register error even if the meaning is clear.

review.q: Where does the chapter say the meaning of a text most often turns?
choices: In the title
In the first sentence
At the tone shift
In the longest paragraph
review.why: The moment the tone changes, marked by a but, a question or a change in sentence length, is where the argument happens.

review.q: Which is the best advice for developing your own voice, according to the chapter?
choices: Use as much slang as possible
Read aloud and replace borrowed phrases with words you would actually say
Never write a short sentence
Copy Twain's sentences word for word
review.why: Voice is built by subtraction first, cutting the costume words, and then by choosing rhythm and attitude on purpose.
